stimulus.text:
“Without some alteration in our political creed, the superstructure we have been seven years raising at the expence of much blood and treasure, must fall. We are fast verging to anarchy and confusion! . . . Thirteen sovereignties pulling against each other, and all tugging at the Federal head, will soon bring ruin on the whole; whereas a liberal and energetic Constitution, well guarded and closely watched, to prevent encroachments, might restore us to that degree of respectability and consequence, to which we are entitled.”

—George Washington to James Madison, Mount Vernon, November 5, 1786
stimulus.source_note: George Washington to James Madison, Mount Vernon, November 5, 1786. Public domain.

books.section: Topic 3.8 The Constitutional Convention and Debates over Ratification

primary_sources: George Washington to James Madison, November 5, 1786

stem: Americans who shared Washington's outlook in this letter would most likely have taken which of the following later positions?

options.text: They would have urged the United States to honor the 1778 alliance by joining France's war against Britain in 1793
options.misconception: Washington did the opposite in 1793, issuing the Proclamation of Neutrality to keep the United States out of France's war.

options.text: They would have opposed chartering the Bank of the United States in 1791
options.misconception: Washington signed the Bank bill into law in 1791, after Hamilton persuaded him it was constitutional.

options.text: They would have supported ratification of the Constitution in 1787–1788
They would have opposed the Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798
options.misconception: The Alien and Sedition Acts were backed by the Federalists, the political heirs of Washington's strong-government outlook.

rationales.C: Washington's letter calls for a liberal and energetic Constitution to replace a system verging on anarchy, which is the case for ratification. Background: he presided over the Philadelphia Convention and lent his prestige to the ratification fight.
rationales.A: Background: Washington kept the United States out of France's war in 1793 with the Proclamation of Neutrality.
rationales.B: Background: Washington signed the Bank bill in 1791, and his supporters backed the Bank, not opposed it.
rationales.D: Background: the Alien and Sedition Acts were Federalist measures, backed by the heirs of Washington's outlook.
rationales.general:
1. Washington's remedy in the letter is a liberal and energetic Constitution.
2. Background: that remedy is exactly what the Philadelphia Convention produced the next summer.
3. Background: Washington presided over the Convention and supported ratification in 1787–1788.
4. Someone sharing his outlook would have backed the Constitution, not the later positions listed.
Remember: match the person's remedy to the later position that carries it out.
